questions.q: Define per capita income and state the formula used to calculate it.
questions.a: Per capita income = Total National Income / Total Population. A wrong answer (e.g., "total income of the country" or "average income of the rich") reveals the student confuses aggregate with average, or thinks per capita refers to a specific group rather than the entire population — a fundamental error that makes all subsequent limitations meaningless.

questions.q: Two countries, X and Y, have identical per capita income of $10,000. In Country X, the richest 10% earn 50% of total income; in Country Y, the richest 10% earn 20%. Explain why per capita income alone cannot distinguish their development levels.
questions.a: Per capita income is an *average* that masks distribution. Country X has extreme inequality — most citizens live on far less than $10,000 — while Country Y's income is more evenly spread, so a typical citizen in Y enjoys better access to nutrition, education, and healthcare. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are equally developed because average is same") shows the student treats the mean as representative of the typical experience, ignoring skewness — a classic board-exam trap.

questions.q: State A has per capita income ₹1,20,000 and infant mortality rate (IMR) 12; State B has per capita income ₹1,18,000 and IMR 45. Using only these two indicators, argue which state has better development outcomes and why per capita income failed to predict it.
questions.a: State A has better development outcomes despite marginally lower per capita income because IMR reflects healthcare access, nutrition, sanitation, and female literacy — non-income dimensions per capita income ignores. Per capita income failed because it measures only monetary flow, not conversion of income into capabilities. A wrong answer choosing State B because "higher income means better development" reveals the student equates income with well-being, missing the core limitation.

questions.q:
Compare the following data for two hypothetical states and identify *three* specific limitations of per capita income illustrated by the data:

| Indicator | State P | State Q |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| Per Capita Income (₹) | 1,50,000 | 1,50,000 |
| Literacy Rate (%) | 95 | 65 |
| Forest Cover (% of area) | 30 | 10 |
| Groundwater Depletion (cm/yr) | 2 | 25 |
questions.a: 1. **Ignores non-income welfare**: Same income but 30% literacy gap shows income doesn't guarantee education. 2. **Ignores environmental sustainability**: State Q depletes groundwater 12× faster and has ⅓ the forest cover — current income comes at future cost. 3. **Ignores inequality within**: Averages hide that State Q's income may be concentrated in water-intensive industries benefiting few. A wrong answer listing only "inequality" or "pollution" without linking to *specific data columns* shows superficial reading — board exams demand data-linked reasoning.

questions.q: "Per capita income is a useless indicator and should be abandoned." Evaluate this statement with two arguments for and two against, using the concept of *necessary but not sufficient* condition.
questions.a: **For**: (1) It ignores distribution, so a country with high per capita income can have widespread poverty. (2) It omits health, education, environment — core to human development. **Against**: (1) It is *necessary* — without minimum income, public facilities (health, schools) cannot be funded; Kerala's high HDI rests on historic public spending enabled by revenue. (2) It is comparable, timely, and universally available — unlike HDI which has data lags. A wrong answer taking an extreme position ("completely useless" or "perfectly adequate") fails the "evaluate" command — board marks require balanced judgment.

questions.q: Construct a 4-indicator "Development Dashboard" for your district that fixes the limitations of per capita income. Justify each indicator in one sentence.
questions.a: Example dashboard: (1) **Median household income** — captures typical experience, not skewed average. (2) **Under-5 mortality rate** — reflects nutrition, healthcare, sanitation combined. (3) **Female literacy rate (15+)** — proxy for gender equity, child health, future earnings. (4) **Groundwater level change (m/yr)** — measures environmental sustainability of current livelihoods. A poor answer lists only income-related indicators (e.g., "GDP, employment, wages") showing the student hasn't internalized *non-monetary* dimensions — the central lesson of this node.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Per capita income?
questions.a: Students believe "higher per capita income automatically means better development" and write in exams: *"Punjab is more developed than Kerala because its per capita income is higher."* This is factually wrong (Kerala's HDI > Punjab's) and conceptually wrong — they confuse *mean income* with *capability expansion*.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least four distinct limitations of per capita income using real data, explain why each limitation matters for policy decisions, and compare two countries/states with similar per capita income but different development outcomes using HDI components.
